claim: Two loss-of-function alleles of sax-3 (yad10 and yad147) were isolated in an unbiased genetic screen for glial migration.
source: In an unbiased genetic screen for glial migration, we isolated two loss-of-function alleles of sax-3, the only Robo receptor in C. elegans (Zallen et al., 1998), with defects in AMsh glial migration.
evidence: The text directly states the isolation of two alleles in a genetic screen, supported by citation to prior work identifying sax-3 as the only Robo receptor.

claim: sax-3 is the only Robo receptor in C. elegans.
source: In an unbiased genetic screen for glial migration, we isolated two loss-of-function alleles of sax-3, the only Robo receptor in C. elegans (Zallen et al., 1998), with defects in AMsh glial migration.
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by citation to Zallen et al., 1998.

claim: AMsh cell bodies reside at the side of and align with the center of pharyngeal terminal bulbs in day 1 (D1) young adults.
source: To quantify the migration of AMsh, we used the pharyngeal terminal bulb as a reference point and found that AMsh cell bodies reside at the side of and align with the center of pharyngeal terminal bulbs in day 1 (D1) young adults (Figure 1a and b).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by reference to Figure 1a and b showing the positioning.

claim: AMsh glia fail to migrate to their final positions in both sax-3(lf) alleles.
source: AMsh glia fail to migrate to their final positions in both sax-3(lf) alleles, and yad10 animals display stronger phenotypes than yad147 animals and show a similar extent of defects as those in the null allele of sax-3 (ky123) (Zallen et al., 1998), suggesting that yad10 is likely a null allele of sax-3 (Figure 1a and b and Figure 1—figure supplement 1a and c).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by data shown in Figure 1a and b and Figure 1—figure supplement 1a and c.

claim: yad10 animals display stronger AMsh migration phenotypes than yad147 animals.
source: AMsh glia fail to migrate to their final positions in both sax-3(lf) alleles, and yad10 animals display stronger phenotypes than yad147 animals and show a similar extent of defects as those in the null allele of sax-3 (ky123) (Zallen et al., 1998), suggesting that yad10 is likely a null allele of sax-3 (Figure 1a and b and Figure 1—figure supplement 1a and c).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by data in Figure 1a and b and Figure 1—figure supplement 1a and c.

claim: yad10 is likely a null allele of sax-3.
source: AMsh glia fail to migrate to their final positions in both sax-3(lf) alleles, and yad10 animals display stronger phenotypes than yad147 animals and show a similar extent of defects as those in the null allele of sax-3 (ky123) (Zallen et al., 1998), suggesting that yad10 is likely a null allele of sax-3 (Figure 1a and b and Figure 1—figure supplement 1a and c).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the comparison of phenotypes between yad10 and the known null allele ky123, supported by data in figures.

claim: sax-3(lf) animals exhibited migration defects in all post-embryonic stages.
source: To further characterize the sax-3(lf) phenotype we examined AMsh migration at different developmental stages in a single animal and found that sax-3(lf) animals exhibited migration defects in all post-embryonic stages, suggesting that sax-3 is required for AMsh migration during development (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1b.

claim: sax-3 is required for AMsh migration during development.
source: To further characterize the sax-3(lf) phenotype we examined AMsh migration at different developmental stages in a single animal and found that sax-3(lf) animals exhibited migration defects in all post-embryonic stages, suggesting that sax-3 is required for AMsh migration during development (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation of migration defects across all post-embryonic stages, supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Loss-of-function of slt-1 (ok255, null allele) did not cause any AMsh migration defects.
source: Next, we examined the function of the canonical Robo ligand, Slit, in AMsh migration and found that loss-of-function of slt-1(ok255, null allele), the only Slit in C. elegans, did not cause any defects, suggesting that Robo functions in a Slit-independent manner to regulate AMsh migration (Figure 1c).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: slt-1 is the only Slit in C. elegans.
source: Next, we examined the function of the canonical Robo ligand, Slit, in AMsh migration and found that loss-of-function of slt-1(ok255, null allele), the only Slit in C. elegans, did not cause any defects, suggesting that Robo functions in a Slit-independent manner to regulate AMsh migration (Figure 1c).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text.

claim: Robo functions in a Slit-independent manner to regulate AMsh migration.
source: Next, we examined the function of the canonical Robo ligand, Slit, in AMsh migration and found that loss-of-function of slt-1(ok255, null allele), the only Slit in C. elegans, did not cause any defects, suggesting that Robo functions in a Slit-independent manner to regulate AMsh migration (Figure 1c).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that slt-1 loss-of-function does not cause defects while sax-3 loss-of-function does, supported by data in Figure 1c.

claim: AMsh cell bodies reside posterior to the nerve ring in control animals.
source: To exclude this possibility, we examined the relative position of AMsh glial cells and the nerve ring. Results show that AMsh cell bodies reside posterior to the nerve ring in control animals but are misplaced anterior to the nerve ring in sax-3(lf) animals (Figure 1—figure supplement 1d and e), suggesting that the AMsh migration defect is not a side phenotype coming from a displaced nerve ring.
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1d and e.

claim: AMsh cell bodies are misplaced anterior to the nerve ring in sax-3(lf) animals.
source: To exclude this possibility, we examined the relative position of AMsh glial cells and the nerve ring. Results show that AMsh cell bodies reside posterior to the nerve ring in control animals but are misplaced anterior to the nerve ring in sax-3(lf) animals (Figure 1—figure supplement 1d and e), suggesting that the AMsh migration defect is not a side phenotype coming from a displaced nerve ring.
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1d and e.

claim: The AMsh migration defect is not a side phenotype coming from a displaced nerve ring.
source: To exclude this possibility, we examined the relative position of AMsh glial cells and the nerve ring. Results show that AMsh cell bodies reside posterior to the nerve ring in control animals but are misplaced anterior to the nerve ring in sax-3(lf) animals (Figure 1—figure supplement 1d and e), suggesting that the AMsh migration defect is not a side phenotype coming from a displaced nerve ring.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that AMsh cells are anterior to the nerve ring in mutants, supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1d and e.

claim: About 40% of sax-3(lf) animals display defects in head morphogenesis, called 'vab head'.
source: As about 40% of sax-3(lf) animals display defects in head morphogenesis, called 'vab head' (Ghenea et al., 2005), it is also possible that AMsh defects could be a result of abnormal head morphology.
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by citation to Ghenea et al., 2005.

claim: sax-3(lf) animals without 'vab head' phenotypes displayed the same degree of AMsh defects as in all sax-3(lf) animals.
source: To rule out this possibility, we examined sax-3(lf) animals without 'vab head' phenotypes and found that they displayed the same degree of AMsh defects as in all sax-3(lf) animals, supporting the conclusion that the AMsh migration defects in sax-3(lf) animals are independent of the 'vab head' phenotypes (Figure 1c).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: The AMsh migration defects in sax-3(lf) animals are independent of the 'vab head' phenotypes.
source: To rule out this possibility, we examined sax-3(lf) animals without 'vab head' phenotypes and found that they displayed the same degree of AMsh defects as in all sax-3(lf) animals, supporting the conclusion that the AMsh migration defects in sax-3(lf) animals are independent of the 'vab head' phenotypes (Figure 1c).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that AMsh defects occur regardless of vab head phenotype, supported by data in Figure 1c.

claim: sax-3 does not function cell-autonomously in AMsh migration.
source: Unexpectedly, as a well-studied receptor, sax-3 does not function cell-autonomously in AMsh migration, and instead expression of sax-3 cDNA in neurons fully rescues sax-3(lf) AMsh phenotypes (Figure 1d, Figure 1—figure supplement 1g).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by rescue experiments shown in Figure 1d and Figure 1—figure supplement 1g.

claim: Expression of sax-3 cDNA in neurons fully rescues sax-3(lf) AMsh phenotypes.
source: Unexpectedly, as a well-studied receptor, sax-3 does not function cell-autonomously in AMsh migration, and instead expression of sax-3 cDNA in neurons fully rescues sax-3(lf) AMsh phenotypes (Figure 1d, Figure 1—figure supplement 1g).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by data shown in Figure 1d and Figure 1—figure supplement 1g.

claim: Expression of truncated forms of SAX-3 lacking the intracellular domains (ΔC) fully rescues sax-3 AMsh defects.
source: It is even more striking that expression of truncated forms of SAX-3 lacking the intracellular domains (ΔC) or both intracellular and transmembrane domains (Δ[C+TM]) fully rescues sax-3 AMsh defects (Figure 1d, Figure 1—figure supplement 1h), while these transgenes did not affect the sax-3(lf) 'vab head' phenotypes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1f and h).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by data shown in Figure 1d and Figure 1—figure supplement 1h.

claim: Expression of truncated forms of SAX-3 lacking both intracellular and transmembrane domains (Δ[C+TM]) fully rescues sax-3 AMsh defects.
source: It is even more striking that expression of truncated forms of SAX-3 lacking the intracellular domains (ΔC) or both intracellular and transmembrane domains (Δ[C+TM]) fully rescues sax-3 AMsh defects (Figure 1d, Figure 1—figure supplement 1h), while these transgenes did not affect the sax-3(lf) 'vab head' phenotypes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1f and h).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by data shown in Figure 1d and Figure 1—figure supplement 1h.

claim: Truncated SAX-3 transgenes (ΔC and Δ[C+TM]) did not affect the sax-3(lf) 'vab head' phenotypes.
source: It is even more striking that expression of truncated forms of SAX-3 lacking the intracellular domains (ΔC) or both intracellular and transmembrane domains (Δ[C+TM]) fully rescues sax-3 AMsh defects (Figure 1d, Figure 1—figure supplement 1h), while these transgenes did not affect the sax-3(lf) 'vab head' phenotypes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1f and h).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1f and h.

claim: Drosophila and human Robo have been shown to be cleaved at the FN3 repeats of the extracellular region.
source: Interestingly, Drosophila and human Robo have been shown to be cleaved at the FN3 repeats of the extracellular region (Coleman et al., 2010; Seki et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by citations to Coleman et al., 2010 and Seki et al., 2010.

claim: FN3 repeats are highly conserved between C. elegans SAX-3 and Drosophila Robo.
source: As FN3 repeats are highly conserved between C. elegans SAX-3 and Drosophila Robo, we decided to test whether SAX-3 could also be cleaved in the extracellular region.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text.

claim: A cleavage fragment of SAX-3 around 70 kDa was detected in different transgene lines.
source: As shown in Figure 2a and Figure 2—figure supplement 1a, we were able to detect a cleavage fragment around 70 kDa in different transgene lines and using different anti-HA antibodies.
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by data shown in Figure 2a and Figure 2—figure supplement 1a.

claim: Based on the molecular weight (about 70 kDa) the cleavage site is likely to be in the FN3 repeats.
source: As the HA tag is fused to the C-terminus of SAX-3, based on the molecular weight (about 70 kDa) the cleavage site is likely to be in the FN3 repeats, which is consistent with what was found in Drosophila Robo (Coleman et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the molecular weight of the cleavage fragment and comparison to Drosophila Robo, supported by citation to Coleman et al., 2010.

claim: The extracellular cleavage of SAX-3 happens from the embryonic 1.5-fold stage to early larval stages.
source: More importantly, the extracellular cleavage happens from the embryonic 1.5-fold stage to early larval stages, when AMsh glia migrate from their birthplace to the nerve ring region (Figure 2a and Figure 2—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by data shown in Figure 2a and Figure 2—figure supplement 1a.

claim: The cleavage of SAX-3 was not regulated by Slit.
source: As the function of sax-3 in AMsh migration is independent of Slit, we asked whether the cleavage of SAX-3 relied on Slit and found that the cleavage of SAX-3 was not regulated by Slit (Figure 2b and Figure 2—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by data shown in Figure 2b and Figure 2—figure supplement 1b.

claim: FN3 repeats were sufficient for the cleavage of SAX-3.
source: We found that FN3 repeats were sufficient for the cleavage (Figure 2c), and based on the molecular weights of free GFP (27 kDa), GFP-FN3-TM (~80 kDa), and the cleavage product (~45 kDa) we concluded that the cleavage site was in the second repeat of FN3.
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: The cleavage site of SAX-3 was in the second repeat of FN3.
source: We found that FN3 repeats were sufficient for the cleavage (Figure 2c), and based on the molecular weights of free GFP (27 kDa), GFP-FN3-TM (~80 kDa), and the cleavage product (~45 kDa) we concluded that the cleavage site was in the second repeat of FN3.
evidence: The claim is inferred from molecular weight analysis of cleavage products, supported by data in Figure 2c.

claim: The cleavage was abolished if the second FN3 repeat was absent.
source: We found that the cleavage was abolished if the second FN3 repeat was absent, while deletion of the third FN3 repeat did not affect the cleavage (Figure 2d).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by data shown in Figure 2d.

claim: Deletion of the third FN3 repeat did not affect the cleavage of SAX-3.
source: We found that the cleavage was abolished if the second FN3 repeat was absent, while deletion of the third FN3 repeat did not affect the cleavage (Figure 2d).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by data shown in Figure 2d.

claim: Extracellular cleavage was undetectable in transgenes expressing a truncated form of SAX-3 without the second FN3 repeat.
source: Consistent with its important role in SAX-3 cleavage, extracellular cleavage was undetectable in transgenes expressing a truncated form of SAX-3 without the second FN3 repeat (Figure 2e).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by data shown in Figure 2e.

claim: The truncated form of SAX-3 that lacks the second FN3 repeat completely lost rescue ability for AMsh migration.
source: To test whether the extracellular cleavage of SAX-3 is essential for its function in AMsh migration, we examined the rescue ability of the truncated form of SAX-3 that lacks the second FN3 repeat and found that this mutant form of SAX-3 completely lost rescue ability (Figure 2f, Figure 2—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by data shown in Figure 2f and Figure 2—figure supplement 1c.

claim: SAX-3 ΔFN3-b fully rescued sax-3(lf) 'vab head' phenotypes.
source: The extracellular cleavage of SAX-3 appears to show certain specificity for AMsh migration, as the same transgene (SAX-3 ΔFN3-b) fully rescued sax-3(lf) 'vab head' phenotypes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1f, Figure 2—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1f and Figure 2—figure supplement 1c.

claim: sax-3(yad175) is a deletion allele that lacks the second repeat of FN3 (FN3-b).
source: To further confirm the role of extracellular SAX-3 cleavage in AMsh migration, we generated a sax-3(yad175) deletion allele that lacks the second repeat of FN3 (FN3-b).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text.

claim: sax-3(yad175) decreases sax-3 mRNA to about 50% of that in control animals.
source: sax-3(yad175) decreases sax-3 mRNA to about 50% of that in control animals (Figure 2—figure supplement 1d) and appears to be a weak loss-of-function allele of sax-3, as both sax-3(ky123, presumptive null allele) and sax-3(yad10) show higher penetrance of vab head and AVM guidance defects (Zallen et al., 1999; Figure 1—figure supplement 1f and Figure 2—figure supplement 1e).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1d.

claim: sax-3(yad175) appears to be a weak loss-of-function allele of sax-3.
source: sax-3(yad175) decreases sax-3 mRNA to about 50% of that in control animals (Figure 2—figure supplement 1d) and appears to be a weak loss-of-function allele of sax-3, as both sax-3(ky123, presumptive null allele) and sax-3(yad10) show higher penetrance of vab head and AVM guidance defects (Zallen et al., 1999; Figure 1—figure supplement 1f and Figure 2—figure supplement 1e).
evidence: The claim is inferred from comparison of phenotypes with other alleles, supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1f and Figure 2—figure supplement 1e and citation to Zallen et al., 1999.

claim: sax-3(yad175) exhibits stronger AMsh migration defects when compared with any other sax-3 alleles examined.
source: Despite being a weak allele, sax-3(yad175) exhibits stronger AMsh migration defects when compared with any other sax-3 alleles examined, supporting the critical role of SAX-3 extracellular cleavage in AMsh migration (Figure 2f).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by data shown in Figure 2f.

claim: A secreted SAX-3 extracellular fragment containing Ig 1–5 domains and the first FN3 repeat (FN3-a) was able to fully rescue sax-3(lf) AMsh defects.
source: To illustrate the function of the extracellular cleavage fragment, we expressed a secreted SAX-3 extracellular fragment containing Ig 1–5 domains and the first FN3 repeat (FN3-a) under pan-neuronal (Punc-33 and Prgef-1) or amphid neuron-specific (Parl-13) promoters, which mimics the cleavage product, and found that this fragment was able to fully rescue sax-3(lf) AMsh defects (Figure 2f, Figure 2—figure supplement 1f).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by data shown in Figure 2f and Figure 2—figure supplement 1f.

claim: Both Ig domains and the first FN3 repeat (FN3-a) may be important for the function of the SAX-3 extracellular cleavage fragment in AMsh migration.
source: Further experiments show that both Ig domains and the first FN3 repeat (FN3-a) may be important for the function of the SAX-3 extracellular cleavage fragment in AMsh migration (Figure 2f).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by data shown in Figure 2f.

claim: The extracellular cleavage fragment but not the full-length SAX-3 can bind with SYG-1::HA.
source: As shown in Figure 3b, the extracellular cleavage fragment but not the full-length SAX-3 can bind with SYG-1::HA, suggesting that SYG-1 can directly or indirectly bind with the SAX-3 extracellular cleavage fragment.
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: SYG-1 can directly or indirectly bind with the SAX-3 extracellular cleavage fragment.
source: As shown in Figure 3b, the extracellular cleavage fragment but not the full-length SAX-3 can bind with SYG-1::HA, suggesting that SYG-1 can directly or indirectly bind with the SAX-3 extracellular cleavage fragment.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the binding data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: syg-1 was expressed in AMsh glia during migration.
source: With these findings, we further examined the function of syg-1 in AMsh migration and found that syg-1 was expressed in AMsh glia during migration and loss-of-function of syg-1(ok3640, null allele) caused similar AMsh migration defects as those in sax-3(lf) mutants (Figure 3c–e, Figure 3—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by data shown in Figure 3c–e and Figure 3—figure supplement 2a.

claim: Loss-of-function of syg-1(ok3640, null allele) caused similar AMsh migration defects as those in sax-3(lf) mutants.
source: With these findings, we further examined the function of syg-1 in AMsh migration and found that syg-1 was expressed in AMsh glia during migration and loss-of-function of syg-1(ok3640, null allele) caused similar AMsh migration defects as those in sax-3(lf) mutants (Figure 3c–e, Figure 3—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by data shown in Figure 3c–e and Figure 3—figure supplement 2a.

claim: Double mutants of syg-1;sax-3 displayed the same extent of defects as in sax-3 single mutants.
source: Furthermore, double mutants of syg-1;sax-3 displayed the same extent of defects as in sax-3 single mutants (Figure 3d and e), supporting the conclusion that syg-1 and sax-3 function in the same genetic pathway to regulate AMsh migration.
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by data shown in Figure 3d and e.

claim: syg-1 and sax-3 function in the same genetic pathway to regulate AMsh migration.
source: Furthermore, double mutants of syg-1;sax-3 displayed the same extent of defects as in sax-3 single mutants (Figure 3d and e), supporting the conclusion that syg-1 and sax-3 function in the same genetic pathway to regulate AMsh migration.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the double mutant analysis, supported by data in Figure 3d and e.

claim: syg-1 has been shown to function together with syg-2 in synapse formation and axon branching.
source: As syg-1 has been shown to function together with syg-2, another Ig super family protein, in synapse formation and axon branching (Shen et al., 2004; Chia et al., 2014), we examined the function of syg-2 in AMsh migration and did not observe any abnormalities in syg-2(lf) mutants (Figure 3e).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by citations to Shen et al., 2004 and Chia et al., 2014.

claim: syg-2(lf) mutants did not show any abnormalities in AMsh migration.
source: As syg-1 has been shown to function together with syg-2, another Ig super family protein, in synapse formation and axon branching (Shen et al., 2004; Chia et al., 2014), we examined the function of syg-2 in AMsh migration and did not observe any abnormalities in syg-2(lf) mutants (Figure 3e).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by data shown in Figure 3e.

claim: syg-1 cell autonomously regulates AMsh migration.
source: Consistent with its potential role as a receptor for the SAX-3 cleavage fragment, syg-1 cell autonomously regulates AMsh migration (Figure 3e, Figure 3—figure supplement 2b).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by data shown in Figure 3e and Figure 3—figure supplement 2b.

claim: The conserved WIRS (WAVE Regulatory receptor sequence) in the SYG-1 C-terminal is essential for its function in AMsh migration.
source: Further genetic analysis also showed that the conserved WIRS (WAVE Regulatory receptor sequence) in the SYG-1 C-terminal (Chia et al., 2014) is essential for its function in AMsh migration (Figure 3e), and interruption of WAVE complex function by mutating gex-3, one of the key components of the WAVE complex (Chia et al., 2014), cell autonomously caused similar AMsh migration defects as observed in sax-3(lf) and syg-1(lf) mutants (Figure 3f,g).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by data shown in Figure 3e and citation to Chia et al., 2014.

claim: Interruption of WAVE complex function by mutating gex-3 cell autonomously caused similar AMsh migration defects as observed in sax-3(lf) and syg-1(lf) mutants.
source: Further genetic analysis also showed that the conserved WIRS (WAVE Regulatory receptor sequence) in the SYG-1 C-terminal (Chia et al., 2014) is essential for its function in AMsh migration (Figure 3e), and interruption of WAVE complex function by mutating gex-3, one of the key components of the WAVE complex (Chia et al., 2014), cell autonomously caused similar AMsh migration defects as observed in sax-3(lf) and syg-1(lf) mutants (Figure 3f,g).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by data shown in Figure 3f,g and citation to Chia et al., 2014.

claim: Expression of the cleavage product of SAX-3 in the tail neurons (Pitr-1b) or tail hypodermis (Plin-44) of sax-3(lf) animals caused AMsh glia to migrate almost three times the distance of control animals.
source: Finally, to further test the ligand/receptor function of the SAX-3 cleavage fragment and SYG-1, we tested whether AMsh glia can further migrate along the body in transgenic animals that express the cleavage product of SAX-3 in the tail neurons (Pitr-1b) or tail hypodermis (Plin-44) of sax-3(lf) animals (Ou et al., 2010). We found that in these transgenes the migration distance of AMsh was almost three times that of control animals, and loss-of-function in syg-1 completely blocked the over-migration phenotypes in these transgenes (Figure 3h and i).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by data shown in Figure 3h and i and citation to Ou et al., 2010.

claim: Loss-of-function in syg-1 completely blocked the over-migration phenotypes caused by ectopic expression of SAX-3 cleavage product.
source: Finally, to further test the ligand/receptor function of the SAX-3 cleavage fragment and SYG-1, we tested whether AMsh glia can further migrate along the body in transgenic animals that express the cleavage product of SAX-3 in the tail neurons (Pitr-1b) or tail hypodermis (Plin-44) of sax-3(lf) animals (Ou et al., 2010). We found that in these transgenes the migration distance of AMsh was almost three times that of control animals, and loss-of-function in syg-1 completely blocked the over-migration phenotypes in these transgenes (Figure 3h and i).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by data shown in Figure 3h and i.

claim: The neuron-released SAX-3 extracellular cleavage fragment functions as an attractive cue, and SYG-1 functions as its receptor to mediate AMsh migration.
source: With this evidence we believe that the neuron-released SAX-3 extracellular cleavage fragment functions as an attractive cue, and SYG-1 functions as its receptor to mediate AMsh migration (Figure 4).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by the cumulative evidence presented and illustrated in Figure 4.

claim: Robo functions as the receptor for the repulsive guidance cue Slit.
source: Studies in different organisms show that Robo functions as the receptor for the repulsive guidance cue Slit (Dickson and Gilestro, 2006), and loss-of-function in Robo causes many phenotypes that are shared by Slit mutants (Dickson and Gilestro, 2006).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by citation to Dickson and Gilestro, 2006.

claim: Loss-of-function in Robo causes many phenotypes that are shared by Slit mutants.
source: Studies in different organisms show that Robo functions as the receptor for the repulsive guidance cue Slit (Dickson and Gilestro, 2006), and loss-of-function in Robo causes many phenotypes that are shared by Slit mutants (Dickson and Gilestro, 2006).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by citation to Dickson and Gilestro, 2006.

claim: Some Robo-mutant phenotypes are not related to Slit.
source: However, genetic studies also showed that some Robo-mutant phenotypes are not related to Slit (Zallen et al., 1998; Hao et al., 2001; Fricke et al., 2001; Hivert et al., 2002; Liu et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: sax-3(lf) animals display many phenotypes that are not observed in slt-1 mutants, including embryonic lethality, abnormal head morphology (vab head), and misplacement of neurons.
source: In C. elegans, there is only one Robo, sax-3, and one Slit, slt-1. sax-3(lf) animals display many phenotypes that are not observed in slt-1 mutants, including embryonic lethality, abnormal head morphology (vab head), and misplacement of neurons (Zallen et al., 1998; Hao et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by citations to Zallen et al., 1998 and Hao et al., 2001.

claim: The extracellular region of Robo is evolutionarily conserved from nematodes to mammals and contains five Ig and three FN3 domains.
source: The extracellular region of Robo is evolutionarily conserved from nematodes to mammals and contains five Ig and three FN3 domains.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text.

claim: The extracellular cleavages of Robo appear to be conserved in C. elegans, Drosophila, and human.
source: The extracellular cleavages of Robo appear to be conserved in C. elegans (this study), Drosophila, and human (Coleman et al., 2010; Seki et al., 2010), though different metalloproteases were utilized in Drosophila and human.
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by citations to Coleman et al., 2010 and Seki et al., 2010.

claim: Different metalloproteases were utilized for Robo cleavage in Drosophila and human.
source: The extracellular cleavages of Robo appear to be conserved in C. elegans (this study), Drosophila, and human (Coleman et al., 2010; Seki et al., 2010), though different metalloproteases were utilized in Drosophila and human.
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by citations to Coleman et al., 2010 and Seki et al., 2010.

claim: The extracellular domains of Robo can dimerize through the Ig domains.
source: Recent biochemical and structural studies show that the extracellular domains of Robo can dimerize through the Ig domains, and the dimerization may be inhibited by the FN3 domain in the absence of Slit (Hivert et al., 2002; Liu et al., 2004; Zakrys et al., 2014; Aleksandrova et al., 2018; Barak et al., 2019; Yamamoto et al., 2019; Pak et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: The dimerization of Robo extracellular domains may be inhibited by the FN3 domain in the absence of Slit.
source: Recent biochemical and structural studies show that the extracellular domains of Robo can dimerize through the Ig domains, and the dimerization may be inhibited by the FN3 domain in the absence of Slit (Hivert et al., 2002; Liu et al., 2004; Zakrys et al., 2014; Aleksandrova et al., 2018; Barak et al., 2019; Yamamoto et al., 2019; Pak et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: The extracellular SAX-3/Robo cleavage fragment lacks the inhibitory second FN3 domain.
source: Since the extracellular SAX-3/Robo cleavage fragment lacks the inhibitory second FN3 domain, it will be expected to strongly bind with itself or with the full length SAX-3/Robo, and these interactions may play a regulatory role in the activation of Robo downstream signals.
